a2-reflexive.title: Reflexive Verbs: me, te, se...
a2-reflexive.explanation: Many everyday Spanish verbs describing routines are reflexive: the action is done TO oneself, so a small pronoun (me/te/se/nos/se) goes right before the verb. "Levantarse" (to get (oneself) up) becomes "me levanto" (I get up), "te levantas" (you get up), "se levanta" (he/she gets up). The pronoun changes with the subject but the verb conjugates completely normally otherwise.
a2-reflexive.fact: Spanish uses reflexive verbs for far more than literal self-actions — "llamarse" (to call oneself) is simply how you say your name ("Me llamo Ana" = "My name is Ana"), and many emotional/change-of-state verbs are reflexive too ("enojarse" = to get angry, "aburrirse" = to get bored) even though English doesn't treat them as reflexive at all.

dialogue.en: What time do you get up?

dialogue.native: Me levanto a las seis y media.
dialogue.en: I get up at six thirty.

a2-preterite.title: The Preterite: Completed Past Actions
a2-preterite.explanation: The preterite describes an action that was completed at a specific point in the past — something that started and finished, like a single event. Regular -ar verbs add -é/-aste/-ó/-amos/-aron (hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablaron); regular -er and -ir verbs share the same endings: -í/-iste/-ió/-imos/-ieron (comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comieron).
a2-preterite.fact: Many of Spanish's most common verbs are irregular in the preterite and simply have to be memorized: "ir" (to go) and "ser" (to be) share the exact same preterite forms (fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fueron) — context alone tells you which one is meant. "Hacer" becomes hice/hiciste/hizo/hicimos/hicieron, and "tener" becomes tuve/tuviste/tuvo/tuvimos/tuvieron.

dialogue.native: Fui al cine con mis amigos.
dialogue.en: I went to the movies with my friends.

a2-imperfect.title: The Imperfect: Ongoing or Habitual Past
a2-imperfect.explanation: While the preterite marks a completed event, the imperfect describes what was ongoing, habitual, or in the background — "used to" or "was ...ing" in English. Regular -ar verbs add -aba/-abas/-aba/-ábamos/-aban (hablaba, hablabas...); -er and -ir verbs share -ía/-ías/-ía/-íamos/-ían (comía, vivía...). Only three verbs are irregular in the imperfect: ser (era, eras, era, éramos, eran), ir (iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, iban), and ver (veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veían).
a2-imperfect.fact: The imperfect is what sets the scene: "Cuando era niño, vivía en el campo" (When I was a child, I lived in the countryside) describes an ongoing state, not a single completed event — that's exactly why "era" and "vivía" are imperfect, not preterite. A sentence often mixes both: the imperfect describes what was happening, and the preterite marks the single event that interrupted it.

a2-ser-estar.title: Ser vs. Estar: Two Ways to Say "To Be"
a2-ser-estar.pattern: ser = identity, characteristics, origin, time · estar = location, condition, ongoing states
a2-ser-estar.explanation: Spanish splits "to be" into two verbs. "Ser" is for things that define what something fundamentally IS: identity ("Soy Ana"), permanent characteristics ("Es alta"), origin ("Es de México"), profession, and time ("Son las tres"). "Estar" is for location ("Estoy en casa") and temporary states or conditions ("Estoy cansado", "La sopa está caliente").
a2-ser-estar.fact: The same adjective can take either verb with a real difference in meaning: "Ella es aburrida" means "She is boring" (a trait), while "Ella está aburrida" means "She is bored" (a temporary feeling) — one small verb swap changes the whole sentence.

dialogue.native: Estoy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú de dónde eres?
dialogue.en: I'm well, thanks. And where are you from?

a2-direct-object.title: Direct Object Pronouns: lo, la, los, las
a2-direct-object.explanation: A direct object pronoun replaces the thing or person directly receiving the action, and in Spanish it goes BEFORE the conjugated verb (the opposite order from English). "Compro el pan" (I buy the bread) becomes "Lo compro" (I buy it) — "pan" is masculine so it's replaced by "lo". Feminine nouns use "la", and the plurals are "los" and "las".
a2-direct-object.fact: With two verbs together (like wanting + an infinitive), the pronoun can go in either of two places with no change in meaning: before the first verb ("Lo quiero comprar") or attached to the end of the infinitive ("Quiero comprarlo") — both mean exactly "I want to buy it".

dialogue.en: Did you already buy the tickets?
Yes, I bought them this morning.

a2-gustar.title: Gustar: "To Be Pleasing To"
a2-gustar.explanation: "Gustar" doesn't work like English "to like" — literally it means "to be pleasing to", so the THING liked is the grammatical subject, and the PERSON who likes it takes an indirect object pronoun. "Me gusta el café" is literally "Coffee is pleasing to me." The verb agrees with the thing liked: "gusta" for one thing, "gustan" for several ("Me gustan los libros").
a2-gustar.fact: Several other very common verbs work exactly the same way: "encantar" (to love/be delighted by), "interesar" (to interest), "molestar" (to bother), "faltar" (to be lacking) — once you understand "me gusta", all of these follow the identical [pronoun] + verb + [thing] pattern.

dialogue.native: Sí, me encanta. Me gustan mucho los partidos los fines de semana.
dialogue.en: Yes, I love it. I really like the games on weekends.

a2-indirect-object.title: Indirect Object Pronouns: me, te, le, nos, les
a2-indirect-object.explanation: An indirect object pronoun marks WHO receives or benefits from an action — usually the person a thing is given, told, or shown to. "Le doy el regalo a mi madre" (I give the gift to my mother) can simply be "Le doy el regalo" once context is clear — "le" already means "to her/him/you-formal". Unlike direct object pronouns, "le" and "les" don't change for gender.
a2-indirect-object.fact: "Le" is ambiguous on its own (it can mean to him, to her, or to you-formal), so Spanish often adds "a él", "a ella", or the person's name for clarity even though the pronoun is technically already there: "Le escribí una carta a mi abuela" keeps both "le" and "a mi abuela" together, which sounds redundant to English speakers but is completely normal and expected in Spanish.

dialogue.en: Did you buy something for your sister?

dialogue.native: Sí, le compré un libro que le va a encantar.
dialogue.en: Yes, I bought her a book that she's going to love.

a2-ir-a.title: Ir a + Infinitive: Talking About the Near Future
a2-ir-a.explanation: The easiest and most common way to talk about future plans in everyday Spanish isn't a special future tense at all — it's just "ir" (to go), conjugated, plus "a", plus an infinitive: "Voy a estudiar" (I am going to study), "Vamos a viajar" (We are going to travel). It works exactly like English "going to".
a2-ir-a.fact: This construction is used constantly in spoken Latin American Spanish — far more often than the formal future tense (like "estudiaré"), which tends to sound a bit more formal or literary in everyday conversation. If you only ever learn one way to talk about the future, "ir a + infinitive" is the one that gets used the most.

dialogue.native: ¿Qué vas a hacer este fin de semana?
dialogue.en: What are you going to do this weekend?

dialogue.native: Voy a visitar a mis padres y vamos a cocinar juntos.
dialogue.en: I am going to visit my parents and we are going to cook together.

a2-comparatives.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
a2-comparatives.explanation: To compare two things, Spanish uses "más...que" (more...than) or "menos...que" (less...than): "Mi hermano es más alto que yo" (My brother is taller than me). For equal comparisons, use "tan...como" (as...as): "Es tan inteligente como su hermana." For the superlative — the most/least of a group — add the definite article: "el más alto", "la más inteligente".
a2-comparatives.fact: A handful of common adjectives have their own irregular comparative words instead of using "más": "bueno" (good) becomes "mejor" (better), "malo" (bad) becomes "peor" (worse), and "viejo"/"joven" have both a regular form (más viejo/más joven) and, for age among people, the special words "mayor"/"menor".

paragraphs.native: Hace un año decidí cambiar de trabajo y mudarme a otra ciudad.
paragraphs.en: A year ago I decided to change jobs and move to another city.

paragraphs.native: Al principio tenía miedo porque no conocía a nadie allí.
paragraphs.en: At first I was afraid because I didn't know anyone there.

paragraphs.native: Poco a poco hice nuevos amigos y aprendí a conocer la ciudad.
paragraphs.en: Little by little I made new friends and learned to know the city.

paragraphs.native: Ahora me siento como en casa y estoy muy feliz con mi decisión.
paragraphs.en: Now I feel at home and I am very happy with my decision.

paragraphs.native: Aprendí que a veces los cambios más difíciles traen las mejores sorpresas.
paragraphs.en: I learned that sometimes the most difficult changes bring the best surprises.

exercises.question: What did the writer decide to do a year ago?
options: Stay the same
Change jobs and move to another city
Retire
Go back to school

exercises.question: Why was the writer afraid at first?
options: They didn't know anyone there
They didn't like the city
They had no money
They didn't like the job

exercises.question: What happened little by little?
options: Nothing changed
They made new friends
They got sicker
They moved again

exercises.question: What did the writer learn?
options: Change is always bad
Difficult changes can bring the best surprises
It's better to never move
Friends are not important
